This voter guide has everything you need to know Supporters pitched Prop. 2 as a common sense solution, noting the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, which advises state lawmakers, has long recommended the state set aside funding for downturns. The measure is endorsed by a bipartisan coalition of groups (https://www.yesonprop2.com/#endorsements), including labor unions, hospital associations and chambers of commerce. “It doubles the size of the state’s rainy day fund and requires California to save more during strong budget years, so we’re not caught flat-footed when the next downturn hits,” wrote (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/10/rainy-day-fund-california-proposition/) Assembly Budget Chair Jesse Gabriel (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/jesse-gabriel-160858), an Encino Democrat, and Assembly Appropriations Vice Chair Josh Hoover (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/josh-hoover-165420), a Folsom Republican and the only GOP lawmaker to vote for the measure. Most Republican lawmakers opposed Prop. 2, stating that the state should use its excess revenue to give taxpayers refunds instead of saving it. They argue that state government already spends too much and that a bigger reserve would merely give state leaders more to spend. “When they say we’re here for fiscal responsibility, it’s like the devil offering a Bible study. Don’t buy it,” said (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/279785#t=685&f=074f023444d682ecc1d857e24642a263) Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014), a San Diego Republican. How long have we had a rainy day fund? Before 2014, California leaders and voters established reserve funds several times (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5028) to weather financial storms, but ended up quickly withdrawing most of those funds, leaving the state with very little savings on hand, according to the legislative analyst. In 2004, following the dot-com bust, voters overwhelmingly supported Prop. 58, a bipartisan ballot measure (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2004-feb-10-me-dems10-story.htm) that required the state to establish a budget stabilization account and make annual deposits into the fund. Sign up for free Δ But lawmakers swiftly depleted the fund during the early months of the Great Recession and were forced to make steep spending cuts, borrow money at expensive rates and use accounting gimmicks to weather the rest of the crisis. Under then-Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, the state Legislature slashed health and welfare funding, scrapped tax credits, furloughed state employees (https://web.archive.org/web/20090809224605/http://www.dpa.ca.gov/news/news/2008/20081106-01.htm) and delayed payments (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2018/3910/recession-recovery-121318.pdf) to schools and local governments. In 2014, as the state’s economy rebounded, then-Gov. Jerry Brown, a Democrat, urged that the state save more. He and the Legislature championed Prop. 2, a bipartisan ballot measure that required the state to save more aggressively and limited when lawmakers could withdraw from the reserves. Nearly 70% of voters approved it. “When the pendulum swings again, we won’t be forced to raise taxes or make the kinds of harsh cuts that were all too common in recent years,” Brown said in a 2014 op-ed (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/Jerry-Brown-preaches-for-Prop-2-by-talking-up-5812922.php) stumping for the reform. The law requires the state to set aside 1.5% of its general fund revenue and any spikes in capital gains tax revenue each year, with half deposited into the reserves and the other half to pay down state debts. It also made it harder for the state to spend the reserves and carved out portions of the savings for schools. Under the law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&division&title&part&chapter&article=XVI), state lawmakers can withdraw from the reserves only when the governor declares a budget emergency and decides that the state is not expected to collect enough revenue in the upcoming fiscal year to match the spending in the three previous budget years. A majority of state lawmakers must vote to ratify the budget emergency. If approved, they are allowed to withdraw up to half of the rainy day fund balance at once, unless they already withdrew half the balance in the previous budget year and still need to take out more. There are no limits on what lawmakers can use the funds for. Bigger reserve = more to spend? Prop. 2 would maintain those withdrawal rules, which critics say would give future governors broad authority to spend down the reserves instead of reining in spending. “The rainy day fund can be invaded even when it’s not raining, simply because spending isn’t as high as it was within the prior three years,” wrote David Crane (https://sfstandard.com/opinion/2026/09/14/newsom-rainy-day-fund-prop-2/), a former economic adviser to Schwarzenegger and founder of Govern for California, a nonprofit fundraising powerhouse (https://calmatters.org/politics/2022/08/california-campaign-finance-donor-network/) that aims to “counter special interest influence.” “Unless the withdrawal rules change, a larger reserve just lets governors bake in spending based on optimistic forecasts, knowing they can always dip into reserves if revenue falls short.” In an interview with CalMatters, Gabriel stressed that voters approved those rules in 2014 and emphasized that the measure has bipartisan support. He also dismissed the criticism that the state should just spend less during downturns, likening it to telling families to eat less or downsize instead of dipping into their savings when they fall on hard times. “I think (the concern) is very misplaced,” he said. “(Prop. 2) is recommended by the experts, because it matches the common-sense wisdom of California families.” READ NEXT What to know about California’s other tax-the-rich measure: Prop. 3 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-3-california/) October 21, 2026 This institute could get $4 billion from a ballot measure. Constitutional Amendment
Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund
Increases the maximum balance of the state’s rainy day reserves from 10% to 20%, changes how deposits and withdrawals from the account are calculated and authorized, exempts deposits from state spending caps, and expands mandatory repayment of certain debts and unfunded liabilities.
SPUR's Recommendation
Given the volatile nature of California’s tax revenue structure, adequate reserve requirements are necessary to avoid severe service reductions during economic downturns. The proposed measure would better manage this boom-and-bust cycle by requiring greater savings during good times to avoid deeper reductions during bad ones — when public safety-net services are most needed.
Vote YES
What Prop. 2 Would Do
Proposition 2 would modify California’s Budget Stabilization Account (the state’s rainy day fund) to
Increase the maximum reserve balance from 10% to 20% of the state’s annual general fund revenues.
Require additional revenue deposits to increase the reserve and repay certain state long-term debts during periods of extraordinary revenue growth.
Expand the definition of long-term debts eligible for repayment from the reserve and extend these requirements from 2030 to 2040.
Clarify the account’s interaction with state constitutional limits on appropriations (setting funds aside for a specific purpose).
The Backstory
California’s tax system produces volatile revenues because it relies heavily on personal income taxes, particularly capital gains. Consequently, revenues rise when the economy and stock market are strong and can fall by billions during downturns, creating boom-and-bust budget cycles. The Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO) notes that these swings are an inherent feature of California’s revenue structure and are likely to continue, making a strong reserve policy an important tool for maintaining stable public services over time. 1
In response, California voters approved Proposition 2 in 2014, establishing a constitutional rainy day reserve known as the Budget Stabilization Account. During strong revenue years, the state must put half of excess revenues into the reserve until the reserve totals 10% of annual General Fund revenues. The other half must be used to pay down specific long-term debts and liabilities through 2030. According to the LAO, Proposition 2 has substantially improved California’s fiscal resilience, allowing the state to build larger reserves that have helped cushion recent budget deficits. 2 Nevertheless, the LAO concludes that the current reserve structure remains insufficient to offset the magnitude of California’s long-term revenue volatility, leaving the state vulnerable to significant budget reductions during prolonged downturns. While California’s reserves have grown, they remain relatively low: the state ranks fifth in the nation for revenue volatility but only twenty-eighth for reserve levels. 3
This election’s Prop. 2 seeks to strengthen California’s reserve framework by increasing both the size of required reserve deposits and the maximum amount the state may accumulate in the reserve. The measure would double the constitutional cap on the reserve from 10% to 20%, require larger deposits to the reserve during years of exceptionally strong capital gains tax revenue growth, broaden the defined debts that may be paid down with other required deposits, and extend these debt payment obligations from 2030 to 2040.
The LAO concludes that these changes would allow California to save substantially more during boom years and better prepare for future recessions, although it also notes that even larger reserves would ultimately provide greater long-term protection against the state’s unusually volatile revenue base. The LAO estimates that the current reserve equal to 10% of revenues would cover about 30% of future budget gaps, while the proposed 20% reserve would cover about half of future gaps.
Finally, Prop. 2 would make several constitutional and procedural changes related to the state appropriations limit established by the Gann Limit, which imposes requirements on how the state can spend General Fund revenues. Under current law, reserve deposits count toward the appropriations limit when made, even though the funds are merely set aside rather than spent. The measure would instead count withdrawals from these accounts (spending), rather than deposits (setting funds aside). This approach better aligns the appropriations limit with the state’s reserve policy by allowing the state to save excess revenues without triggering the spending limit, while ensuring those funds count against the limit when ultimately spent.
The California Legislature placed the measure on the ballot, and it requires a simple majority (50% plus one vote) for approval.
Equity Impacts
Over time, the measure would improve services for vulnerable communities that disproportionately rely on state-administered and state-funded programs. By building reserves during better economic times to minimize state budget reductions during recessions and economic downturns, the state would be better able to meet demand for public safety-net services, which often increases during those periods.
Pros
Prop. 2 would improve the state’s rainy day account requirements to better manage the boom-and-bust nature of the state’s volatile revenue structure, better matching spending and revenues over time.
By improving the stability of the state’s fiscal management, the measure would benefit California city and county governments that often face state budget reductions during economic downturns.
By extending mandatory requirements to pay down debts and long-term liabilities, the measure would reduce the state’s long-term costs.
The measure would rationalize the reserve’s interaction with state constitutional appropriation limit requirements.
Con
The maximum required balance for the Budget Stabilization Account would cover only about 50% of revenue losses during a typical economic downturn.

Consequently, revenues rise when the economy and stock market are strong and can fall by billions during downturns, creating boom-and-bust budget cycles. The Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO) notes that these swings are an inherent feature of California’s revenue structure and are likely to continue, making a strong reserve policy an important tool for maintaining stable public services over time. 1
In response, California voters approved Proposition 2 in 2014, establishing a constitutional rainy day reserve known as the Budget Stabilization Account. During strong revenue years, the state must put half of excess revenues into the reserve until the reserve totals 10% of annual General Fund revenues. The other half must be used to pay down specific long-term debts and liabilities through 2030. According to the LAO, Proposition 2 has substantially improved California’s fiscal resilience, allowing the state to build larger reserves that have helped cushion recent budget deficits. 2 Nevertheless, the LAO concludes that the current reserve structure remains insufficient to offset the magnitude of California’s long-term revenue volatility, leaving the state vulnerable to significant budget reductions during prolonged downturns. While California’s reserves have grown, they remain relatively low: the state ranks fifth in the nation for revenue volatility but only twenty-eighth for reserve levels. 3
This election’s Prop. 2 seeks to strengthen California’s reserve framework by increasing both the size of required reserve deposits and the maximum amount the state may accumulate in the reserve. The measure would double the constitutional cap on the reserve from 10% to 20%, require larger deposits to the reserve during years of exceptionally strong capital gains tax revenue growth, broaden the defined debts that may be paid down with other required deposits, and extend these debt payment obligations from 2030 to 2040.
The LAO concludes that these changes would allow California to save substantially more during boom years and better prepare for future recessions, although it also notes that even larger reserves would ultimately provide greater long-term protection against the state’s unusually volatile revenue base. The LAO estimates that the current reserve equal to 10% of revenues would cover about 30% of future budget gaps, while the proposed 20% reserve would cover about half of future gaps.
Finally, Prop. 2 would make several constitutional and procedural changes related to the state appropriations limit established by the Gann Limit, which imposes requirements on how the state can spend General Fund revenues. Under current law, reserve deposits count toward the appropriations limit when made, even though the funds are merely set aside rather than spent. The measure would instead count withdrawals from these accounts (spending), rather than deposits (setting funds aside). This approach better aligns the appropriations limit with the state’s reserve policy by allowing the state to save excess revenues without triggering the spending limit, while ensuring those funds count against the limit when ultimately spent.
The California Legislature placed the measure on the ballot, and it requires a simple majority (50% plus one vote) for approval.
Equity Impacts
Over time, the measure would improve services for vulnerable communities that disproportionately rely on state-administered and state-funded programs. By building reserves during better economic times to minimize state budget reductions during recessions and economic downturns, the state would be better able to meet demand for public safety-net services, which often increases during those periods.
Pros
Prop. 2 would improve the state’s rainy day account requirements to better manage the boom-and-bust nature of the state’s volatile revenue structure, better matching spending and revenues over time.
By improving the stability of the state’s fiscal management, the measure would benefit California city and county governments that often face state budget reductions during economic downturns.
By extending mandatory requirements to pay down debts and long-term liabilities, the measure would reduce the state’s long-term costs.
The measure would rationalize the reserve’s interaction with state constitutional appropriation limit requirements.
Con
The maximum required balance for the Budget Stabilization Account would cover only about 50% of revenue losses during a typical economic downturn.
Vote YES

Issue Brief
Should Voters Approve Proposition 2? How California’s Rainy Day Fund Would Be Updated
Examining the 2026 Ballot Measure to Strengthen California’s Budget Stabilization Account and Modify the Gann Limit
August 2026 | By Scott Graves (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/scott-graves/), Alissa Anderson (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/alissa-anderson/), and Erik Saucedo
Print Issue Brief
key takeaway
Proposition 2 on the November 2026 ballot would change the rules for California’s rainy day fund to build a larger reserve and better protect core public services during budget emergencies, such as an economic downturn. Prop. 2 also would expand the types of state debt that could be repaid with General Fund revenues that must be set aside each year. In addition, Prop. 2 would modify the relationship between certain reserves and California’s state spending cap, or “Gann Limit” — a change that would allow policymakers to build up reserves in years when revenues are strong and the state is at risk of exceeding the limit. The Legislature placed Prop. 2, a constitutional amendment, on the ballot by passing ACA 20 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20).
table of contents
What Would Proposition 2 Do?
What Would Proposition 2 Not Do?
What Would Proposition 2 Mean for California?
What Would Proposition 2 Do?
Prop. 2 would amend the state Constitution to change several of the rules that govern California’s rainy day fund — the state’s primary budget reserve, known as the Budget Stabilization Account (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/californias-rainy-day-fund-and-other-budget-reserves-overview/) (BSA). 1 (javascript:void(0)) California voters created the BSA in 2004 by passing Prop. 58 and reformed the BSA a decade later by approving Prop. 2 of 2014. For an analysis of Prop. 2 of 2014, see California Budget & Policy Center, Proposition 2: Should California Prioritize Paying Down Debt and Significantly Change State Budget Reserve Policies? (https://calbudgetcenter.org/app/uploads/2022/10/Prop-2-2020-IB.pdf) (September 2014). In addition, Prop. 2 would modestly change the interaction between state reserves and the state spending cap, commonly called the Gann Limit (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/qa-why-hitting-gann-limit-threatens-ongoing-investments-in-californians/). This section highlights the key changes that Prop. 2 would make if approved by voters in November.
Increases the Maximum Size of the Rainy Day Fund (BSA) to 20% of General Fund Revenues
Current Law
The state Constitution limits the size of the BSA to 10% of estimated General Fund tax revenues. 2 (javascript:void(0)) Specifically, the amount transferred to the BSA in any fiscal year may not result in a balance that exceeds 10% of estimated General Fund “proceeds of taxes.” Proceeds of taxes are estimated for the purpose of calculating the State Appropriations Limit (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Detail/4416) (or Gann Limit (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/qa-why-hitting-gann-limit-threatens-ongoing-investments-in-californians/)) and tend to differ slightly from total General Fund revenues and transfers. When this limit is reached, any dollars that otherwise would go into the BSA must be spent on infrastructure.
Proposition 2
Prop. 2 would double the BSA cap to 20% of estimated General Fund tax revenues. If the 20% cap were ever reached, the dollars that would otherwise be deposited into the BSA would instead be spent on infrastructure, as under current law.
Changes How “Excess” Capital Gains Revenues Are Calculated to Save More in Strong Revenue Years
Current Law
The state Constitution requires some General Fund revenues to be set aside annually and requires additional General Fund revenues to be set aside when certain conditions are met. Generally speaking, 50% of these set-aside revenues are deposited into the rainy day fund, and the other 50% are used to pay down certain state debts. 3 (javascript:void(0)) As noted below, some set-aside revenues are owed to TK-14 education through the Prop. 98 minimum funding guarantee. This portion of set-aside revenues is governed by different rules and does not go toward the rainy day fund or state debt payments. These set-aside revenues are determined in two ways:
1.5% of General Fund revenues are automatically set aside every year. For example, if General Fund tax revenues were estimated to total $250 billion for a fiscal year, the state would need to set aside a total of $3.75 billion (1.5%), with half deposited into the rainy day fund (BSA) and the other half used to pay down certain state debts. Prop. 2 would not change this required annual transfer.
In addition to this fixed annual transfer, the state is required to set aside “excess” capital gains revenues. This requirement is triggered in years when estimated General Fund tax revenues that come from personal income taxes on capital gains exceed a specified target: 8% of total General Fund tax revenues. 4 (javascript:void(0)) Capital gains are the profits realized from selling assets that have increased in value, such as stock shares or real estate. Revenues from capital gains can be volatile from year to year depending on market conditions. When this occurs, a portion of these “excess” capital gains revenues — specifically, the share that is not owed to TK-14 education through the Proposition 98 minimum funding guarantee (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/what-is-proposition-98-guaranteed-school-funding-explained/) — is split equally between building the BSA balance and paying down certain state debts. 5 (javascript:void(0)) The share of “excess” capital gains revenues that are owed to TK-14 education via Prop. 98 is subject to a different set of rules. See California Budget & Policy Center, Proposition 2: Should California Prioritize Paying Down Debt and Significantly Change State Budget Reserve Policies? (https://calbudgetcenter.org/app/uploads/2022/10/Prop-2-2020-IB.pdf) (September 2014), p. 2.
Proposition 2
Prop. 2 would change how “excess” capital gains revenues are calculated in order to set aside more revenue for the rainy day fund and state debt payments. Under Prop. 2, there would be two categories of “excess” capital gains revenues, as follows:
The first category of “excess” revenues would include capital gains revenues that total between 8% and 10% of General Fund tax revenues.
The second category of “excess” revenues would equal 1.5 times the portion of capital gains revenues that are above 10% of General Fund tax revenues. For example, if there are $2 billion in capital gains revenues above the 10% threshold, the state would have to set aside a total of $3 billion ($2.0 billion * 1.5) — $1 billion more than is required under current law.
As under current law, the portion of these “excess” revenues that are not owed to TK-14 education through Prop. 98 would be split equally between the rainy day fund and certain state debt payments.
Expands the Types of State Debt That May Be Paid with Set-Aside Revenues
Current Law
The state Constitution requires that half of General Fund revenues set aside each year be used to repay certain state debts. 6 (javascript:void(0)) The revenues used to calculate this 50% requirement exclude set-aside revenues that are owed to TK-14 education through California’s Prop. 98 minimum funding guarantee. Currently, the state may only use these set-aside revenues to 1) prefund state retiree health benefits and/or 2) pay down unfunded liabilities associated with state‑level pension plans. In prior years, the state was allowed to use these set-aside revenues to pay down certain types of budgetary debt . This included payments owed to K-12 schools and community colleges as of July 1, 2014. 7 (javascript:void(0)) These payments went toward unfunded prior-year Prop. 98 obligations, including so-called “settle-up” obligations, which reflect the reconciliation of estimates of the annual Prop. 98 minimum funding level and the actual Prop. 98 guarantee. However, by 2019-20, the state had repaid all of the outstanding budgetary debt (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4887).
Proposition 2
Prop. 2 would update and expand the list of state debts that could be paid with set-aside revenues. Specifically, these funds could be used to:
Repay federal unemployment insurance (UI) loans. Under Prop. 2, revenues set aside for state debt could be used to repay “federal loans made to the Unemployment Fund.” The measure does not specify whether Prop. 2 funds could be used to pay the interest as well as the principal on federal UI loans.
Repay certain TK-14 education obligations. Under Prop. 2, the state could once again use set-aside revenues, during any fiscal year, to make certain payments owed to TK-12 schools and community colleges. 8 (javascript:void(0)) Specifically, Prop. 2 would allow revenues set aside for state debt payments to be used for “unfunded prior fiscal year General Fund obligations” pursuant to the Prop. 98 minimum funding guarantee. These include so-called “settle-up” obligations, which reflect the reconciliation of estimates of the annual Prop. 98 minimum funding level and the actual Prop. 98 guarantee. Under the original Prop. 2 (2014 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/app/uploads/2022/10/Prop-2-2020-IB.pdf)), the state was allowed to use set-aside revenues to pay down unfunded prior fiscal year General Fund obligations pursuant to Prop. 98, but only for debt accrued prior to July 1, 2014. That debt was repaid by the 2019-20 fiscal year. In addition, set-aside revenues could be used to help accelerate the phase-out of an outstanding debt tied to an accounting maneuver that state leaders adopted in the 2023-24 budget (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4929) to address an issue related to the Prop. 98 minimum funding guarantee. 9 (javascript:void(0)) For a discussion of this accounting maneuver, see Legislative Analyst’s Office, The 2024-25 Budget: The Governor’s Proposition 98 Funding Maneuver (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4840) (February 15, 2024).
Repay General Fund loans to the Medi-Cal program. The 2025-26 budget transferred $4.4 billion (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5075) from the state General Fund to the Medical Providers Interim Payment Fund (https://funds.dof.ca.gov/app/download/0201) to help cover higher-than-expected Medi-Cal costs. The budget delayed repayment of this loan, with payments starting in 2027-28 and potentially continuing for several years. Under Prop. 2, revenues set aside for state debt could be used to accelerate the paydown of the 2025-26 Medi-Cal loan or other Medi-Cal loans.
Extends the Debt-Paydown Requirement by 10 Years, to 2039-40
Current Law
The state Constitution requires 50% of set-aside revenues to be used to pay down certain state debts through the 2029-30 state fiscal year. 10 (javascript:void(0)) The revenues used to calculate this 50% requirement exclude set-aside revenues that are owed to TK-14 education through California’s Prop. 98 minimum funding guarantee. Starting in 2030-31, these payments become optional, and any set-aside revenues that are not used to pay down debt must be deposited into the rainy day fund.
Proposition 2
Prop. 2 would require 50% of set-aside revenues to go toward paying down state debts for an additional 10 years ending in 2039-40. 11 (javascript:void(0)) The revenues that would be used to calculate this 50% requirement would continue to exclude set-aside revenues that are owed to TK-14 education through California’s Prop. 98 minimum funding guarantee. Starting in 2040-41, these payments would become optional, and any set-aside revenues that were not used to pay down debt would have to be deposited into the rainy day fund.
Changes the Relationship Between Deposits/Withdrawals and the Gann Limit
Current Law
The state Constitution requires that deposits into state reserves be counted as spending for the purpose of calculations required by California’s spending cap. This is the case even though tax dollars transferred to a reserve clearly will not immediately be spent through the budget. This rule was put in place by Prop. 4 of 1979, which created the state spending cap. 12 (javascript:void(0)) For simplicity, this discussion uses the word “spending.” However, Prop. 4 uses the technical phrase “appropriations subject to limitation.” See California Constitution, Article XIIIB, Section 5 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%205.&article=XIII%20B). This cap is formally known as the State Appropriations Limit (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Detail/4416), but is more commonly called the Gann Limit (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/qa-why-hitting-gann-limit-threatens-ongoing-investments-in-californians/). 13 (javascript:void(0)) The spending cap applies to the state as well as to local governments.
In contrast, withdrawals from state reserves as well as expenditures of withdrawn funds do not count as spending for the purpose of the Gann Limit. 14 (javascript:void(0)) California Constitution, Article XIIIB, Section 5 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%205.&article=XIII%20B). In other words, under current constitutional rules, tax dollars count toward the spending cap when they go into a reserve, but do not count toward the cap when they come out.
As a result, in years when state revenues are growing rapidly and the state is at risk of exceeding the spending cap, state leaders cannot bolster California’s fiscal resilience by further building up reserves, because doing so would put the state over the spending limit. 15 (javascript:void(0)) Revenues that are projected to exceed the spending limit can only be used in a few narrow ways if state leaders want to avoid going over the cap. If the state exceeds the cap for two consecutive years, half must go to taxpayers and the other half must go to TK-14 education on a per-pupil basis.
Proposition 2
Prop. 2 would alter the relationship between deposits/withdrawals and the Gann Limit for two state reserves: the rainy day fund (BSA) and the Projected Surplus Temporary Holding Account.
Prop. 2 would change the interaction between the BSA and the Gann Limit. Under Prop. 2, revenues would not count toward the state spending cap when they go into the rainy day fund, but would count when they are withdrawn.
Prop. 2 would change the interaction between the Projected Surplus Temporary Holding Account and the Gann Limit. The holding account (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/californias-rainy-day-fund-and-other-budget-reserves-overview/#h-projected-surplus-temporary-holding-account-a-place-to-set-aside-anticipated-surplus-revenues) is used to temporarily set aside anticipated surplus revenues for up to one year. Under Prop. 2, revenues deposited into the holding account — up to a cap — would not count toward the Gann Limit, but they would count when they come out. This cap would be equal to 10% of total General Fund tax revenues in the year the transfer is made. For example, if General Fund tax revenues were estimated to total $250 billion, then up to $25 billion could go into the holding account without counting toward the Gann Limit (but would count toward the Gann Limit when withdrawn). However, if the holding account deposit exceeded $25 billion, then the excess amount would count toward the Gann Limit (but would not count when withdrawn).
Changes How a Budget Emergency May Be Declared
Current Law
The state Constitution requires the governor to declare a budget emergency in order to:
Suspend or reduce a required deposit into the rainy day fund (BSA) or the Public Schools System Stabilization Account (PSSSA), or
Withdraw funds from the BSA or the PSSSA. 16 (javascript:void(0)) For a description of the PSSSA, or schools reserve, see California Budget & Policy Center, California’s Rainy Day Fund and Other Budget Reserves Overview (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/californias-rainy-day-fund-and-other-budget-reserves-overview/#h-public-school-system-stabilization-account-psssa-the-reserve-for-k-12-schools-amp-community-colleges) (April 2026).
To declare a budget emergency, the governor signs a proclamation. It may be signed very late in the fiscal year, including after the June 15 constitutional deadline for the Legislature to pass the budget. For example, in 2025, Governor Newsom issued a budget emergency proclamation on June 27 (https://www.gov.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Budget-Proc-2025.pdf) — well after the Legislature passed the budget and just three days before the end of the 2024-25 fiscal year.
This misaligned timing puts the Legislature in the awkward position of passing a budget that assumes a budget emergency before the governor has made it official.
Proposition 2
Prop. 2 would create a simplified pathway for declaring a budget emergency. This alternative pathway is intended to prevent a situation where the governor suggests a budget emergency will be declared, but then fails to issue a proclamation before the Legislature’s June 15 constitutional deadline to pass the budget.
Prop. 2 would allow the governor’s May Revision, which is due out by May 14, to constitute the proclamation of a budget emergency

Critics say it would only allow state leaders to spend more in the future. The question Proposition 2 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-2-rainy-day-fund/) poses to California voters is simple: Should the state be able to save more money when its economy is booming? The ballot measure, dubbed the Save for California’s Future Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca20), seeks to shore up California’s rainy day fund by allowing state lawmakers to sock away up to 20% of the state’s general fund tax revenue — double the current ceiling of 10%. It would also require the state to save a bigger share of the gains when revenue is growing faster. Proponents, including Gov. Gavin Newsom and Democratic lawmakers, say the state needs a bigger savings account to weather its volatile economy. Because California’s tax revenue depends so much on wealthy residents’ stock earnings, the state budget is often caught in a boom-or-bust cycle (https://calmatters.org/explainers/california-budget-whiplash/) at the mercy of the market. In recent years, the state has seen robust tax revenue from an AI-fueled economy, which has helped state leaders avoid or delay painful cuts (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/05/gavin-newsom-final-budget-plan/) to social services even when they projected significant deficits. But economists have consistently warned the boom may not last, and the federal budget cuts to healthcare and welfare programs this year deepened that uncertainty. ELECTION 2026 (https://calmatters.org/tag/election-2026) 2026 Voter Guide (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) Get ready for California’s midterm election. This voter guide has everything you need to know Supporters pitched Prop. 2 as a common sense solution, noting the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, which advises state lawmakers, has long recommended the state set aside funding for downturns. The measure is endorsed by a bipartisan coalition of groups (https://www.yesonprop2.com/#endorsements), including labor unions, hospital associations and chambers of commerce. “It doubles the size of the state’s rainy day fund and requires California to save more during strong budget years, so we’re not caught flat-footed when the next downturn hits,” wrote (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/10/rainy-day-fund-california-proposition/) Assembly Budget Chair Jesse Gabriel (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/jesse-gabriel-160858), an Encino Democrat, and Assembly Appropriations Vice Chair Josh Hoover (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/josh-hoover-165420), a Folsom Republican and the only GOP lawmaker to vote for the measure. Most Republican lawmakers opposed Prop. 2, stating that the state should use its excess revenue to give taxpayers refunds instead of saving it. They argue that state government already spends too much and that a bigger reserve would merely give state leaders more to spend. “When they say we’re here for fiscal responsibility, it’s like the devil offering a Bible study. Don’t buy it,” said (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/279785#t=685&f=074f023444d682ecc1d857e24642a263) Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014), a San Diego Republican. How long have we had a rainy day fund? Before 2014, California leaders and voters established reserve funds several times (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5028) to weather financial storms, but ended up quickly withdrawing most of those funds, leaving the state with very little savings on hand, according to the legislative analyst. In 2004, following the dot-com bust, voters overwhelmingly supported Prop. 58, a bipartisan ballot measure (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2004-feb-10-me-dems10-story.htm) that required the state to establish a budget stabilization account and make annual deposits into the fund. Sign up for free Δ But lawmakers swiftly depleted the fund during the early months of the Great Recession and were forced to make steep spending cuts, borrow money at expensive rates and use accounting gimmicks to weather the rest of the crisis. Under then-Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, the state Legislature slashed health and welfare funding, scrapped tax credits, furloughed state employees (https://web.archive.org/web/20090809224605/http://www.dpa.ca.gov/news/news/2008/20081106-01.htm) and delayed payments (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2018/3910/recession-recovery-121318.pdf) to schools and local governments. In 2014, as the state’s economy rebounded, then-Gov. Jerry Brown, a Democrat, urged that the state save more. He and the Legislature championed Prop. 2, a bipartisan ballot measure that required the state to save more aggressively and limited when lawmakers could withdraw from the reserves. Nearly 70% of voters approved it. “When the pendulum swings again, we won’t be forced to raise taxes or make the kinds of harsh cuts that were all too common in recent years,” Brown said in a 2014 op-ed (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/Jerry-Brown-preaches-for-Prop-2-by-talking-up-5812922.php) stumping for the reform. The law requires the state to set aside 1.5% of its general fund revenue and any spikes in capital gains tax revenue each year, with half deposited into the reserves and the other half to pay down state debts. It also made it harder for the state to spend the reserves and carved out portions of the savings for schools. Under the law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&division&title&part&chapter&article=XVI), state lawmakers can withdraw from the reserves only when the governor declares a budget emergency and decides that the state is not expected to collect enough revenue in the upcoming fiscal year to match the spending in the three previous budget years. A majority of state lawmakers must vote to ratify the budget emergency. If approved, they are allowed to withdraw up to half of the rainy day fund balance at once, unless they already withdrew half the balance in the previous budget year and still need to take out more. There are no limits on what lawmakers can use the funds for. Bigger reserve = more to spend? Prop. 2 would maintain those withdrawal rules, which critics say would give future governors broad authority to spend down the reserves instead of reining in spending. “The rainy day fund can be invaded even when it’s not raining, simply because spending isn’t as high as it was within the prior three years,” wrote David Crane (https://sfstandard.com/opinion/2026/09/14/newsom-rainy-day-fund-prop-2/), a former economic adviser to Schwarzenegger and founder of Govern for California, a nonprofit fundraising powerhouse (https://calmatters.org/politics/2022/08/california-campaign-finance-donor-network/) that aims to “counter special interest influence.” “Unless the withdrawal rules change, a larger reserve just lets governors bake in spending based on optimistic forecasts, knowing they can always dip into reserves if revenue falls short.” In an interview with CalMatters, Gabriel stressed that voters approved those rules in 2014 and emphasized that the measure has bipartisan support. He also dismissed the criticism that the state should just spend less during downturns, likening it to telling families to eat less or downsize instead of dipping into their savings when they fall on hard times. “I think (the concern) is very misplaced,” he said. “(Prop. 2) is recommended by the experts, because it matches the common-sense wisdom of California families.” READ NEXT What to know about California’s other tax-the-rich measure: Prop. 3 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-3-california/) October 21, 2026 This institute could get $4 billion from a ballot measure. Prop
2
CA
Prop
2
|
Constitutional Amendment
Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund
Increases the maximum balance of the state’s rainy day reserves from 10% to 20%, changes how deposits and withdrawals from the account are calculated and authorized, exempts deposits from state spending caps, and expands mandatory repayment of certain debts and unfunded liabilities.
SPUR's Recommendation
Given the volatile nature of California’s tax revenue structure, adequate reserve requirements are necessary to avoid severe service reductions during economic downturns. The proposed measure would better manage this boom-and-bust cycle by requiring greater savings during good times to avoid deeper reductions during bad ones — when public safety-net services are most needed.
Vote YES
What Prop. 2 Would Do
Proposition 2 would modify California’s Budget Stabilization Account (the state’s rainy day fund) to
Increase the maximum reserve balance from 10% to 20% of the state’s annual general fund revenues.
Require additional revenue deposits to increase the reserve and repay certain state long-term debts during periods of extraordinary revenue growth.
Expand the definition of long-term debts eligible for repayment from the reserve and extend these requirements from 2030 to 2040.
Clarify the account’s interaction with state constitutional limits on appropriations (setting funds aside for a specific purpose).
The Backstory
California’s tax system produces volatile revenues because it relies heavily on personal income taxes, particularly capital gains. Consequently, revenues rise when the economy and stock market are strong and can fall by billions during downturns, creating boom-and-bust budget cycles. The Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO) notes that these swings are an inherent feature of California’s revenue structure and are likely to continue, making a strong reserve policy an important tool for maintaining stable public services over time. 1
In response, California voters approved Proposition 2 in 2014, establishing a constitutional rainy day reserve known as the Budget Stabilization Account. During strong revenue years, the state must put half of excess revenues into the reserve until the reserve totals 10% of annual General Fund revenues. The other half must be used to pay down specific long-term debts and liabilities through 2030. According to the LAO, Proposition 2 has substantially improved California’s fiscal resilience, allowing the state to build larger reserves that have helped cushion recent budget deficits. 2 Nevertheless, the LAO concludes that the current reserve structure remains insufficient to offset the magnitude of California’s long-term revenue volatility, leaving the state vulnerable to significant budget reductions during prolonged downturns. While California’s reserves have grown, they remain relatively low: the state ranks fifth in the nation for revenue volatility but only twenty-eighth for reserve levels. 3
This election’s Prop. 2 seeks to strengthen California’s reserve framework by increasing both the size of required reserve deposits and the maximum amount the state may accumulate in the reserve. The measure would double the constitutional cap on the reserve from 10% to 20%, require larger deposits to the reserve during years of exceptionally strong capital gains tax revenue growth, broaden the defined debts that may be paid down with other required deposits, and extend these debt payment obligations from 2030 to 2040.
The LAO concludes that these changes would allow California to save substantially more during boom years and better prepare for future recessions, although it also notes that even larger reserves would ultimately provide greater long-term protection against the state’s unusually volatile revenue base. The LAO estimates that the current reserve equal to 10% of revenues would cover about 30% of future budget gaps, while the proposed 20% reserve would cover about half of future gaps.
Finally, Prop. 2 would make several constitutional and procedural changes related to the state appropriations limit established by the Gann Limit, which imposes requirements on how the state can spend General Fund revenues. Under current law, reserve deposits count toward the appropriations limit when made, even though the funds are merely set aside rather than spent. The measure would instead count withdrawals from these accounts (spending), rather than deposits (setting funds aside). This approach better aligns the appropriations limit with the state’s reserve policy by allowing the state to save excess revenues without triggering the spending limit, while ensuring those funds count against the limit when ultimately spent.
The California Legislature placed the measure on the ballot, and it requires a simple majority (50% plus one vote) for approval.
Equity Impacts
Over time, the measure would improve services for vulnerable communities that disproportionately rely on state-administered and state-funded programs. By building reserves during better economic times to minimize state budget reductions during recessions and economic downturns, the state would be better able to meet demand for public safety-net services, which often increases during those periods.
Pros
Prop. 2 would improve the state’s rainy day account requirements to better manage the boom-and-bust nature of the state’s volatile revenue structure, better matching spending and revenues over time.
By improving the stability of the state’s fiscal management, the measure would benefit California city and county governments that often face state budget reductions during economic downturns.
By extending mandatory requirements to pay down debts and long-term liabilities, the measure would reduce the state’s long-term costs.
The measure would rationalize the reserve’s interaction with state constitutional appropriation limit requirements.
Con
The maximum required balance for the Budget Stabilization Account would cover only about 50% of revenue losses during a typical economic downturn.
Vote YES

assistantMessageEvent.content:
I am reviewing the Budget Center analysis, David Crane's criticisms, and the LAO reserve policy report to complete my research.

I am weighing normative judgment against the evidence. The nonpartisan LAO analysis shows Prop 2 raises the BSA cap to 20% of general fund tax revenues, requires larger deposits when capital gains exceed the prior threshold, extends extra debt payments through 2040, and expands eligible debt to include federal UI loans, Prop 98 settle-ups, and Medi-Cal loans.

Deposits into the BSA and PSTHA do not count toward the Gann limit, but withdrawals do. The May Revision process could also serve as a budget emergency proclamation.

The LAO projects higher reserves and more debt payments under Prop 2. This would ease balancing when revenues decline.

An independent expert consensus supports the change. The LAO report finds the current 10% reserve covers only about 30% of future budget gaps. A 20% reserve would cover roughly half. California ranks fifth in revenue volatility yet twenty-eighth in reserve levels. The current structure is insufficient.

SPUR endorses the proposition.

The Budget & Policy Center, Sacramento Bee, McClatchy, PTA, California Professional Firefighters, hospitals, and the Los Angeles Chamber of Commerce also support the proposition. The SF Chronicle endorses it but warns that politicians must actually use the reserves. One Republican, Josh Hoover, voted yes and co-wrote a support op-ed. Most opposition comes from Republican legislators and groups such as Reform California and the California Policy Center.

David Crane criticizes the withdrawal rules as too loose. He warns that a larger reserve could let governors bake in spending and reduce taxpayer rebates.

The main objection about a slush fund is being evaluated. The withdrawal rules are unchanged from Prop 2 of 2014. A governor must declare a budget emergency. The legislature must approve any withdrawal. Normally only half the balance can be taken out.

The budget emergency declaration is a pre-existing feature, not created by this proposition. A larger reserve does not make withdrawals easier; it simply increases the pool of funds available under the same rules. The alternative of not saving would spend money immediately during boom years, which actually worsens volatility.

The most substantive objection is the Gann limit loophole and its effect on taxpayer rebates.

The Gann limit loophole is being examined more closely. Under current law, reserve deposits count as appropriations subject to the limit, while withdrawals do not. Prop 2 reverses this for BSA and PSTHA. This means surplus years near the limit could be saved rather than refunded to taxpayers or spent on infrastructure. Whether this is harmful is still being weighed.

Taxpayer rebates under the Gann limit are rare. The limit has been modified many times and rarely binds. When it does bind, one-time rebates would sacrifice reserves that protect schools and services during downturns. Schools already have Prop 98 protection and a dedicated reserve. One-time rebates are politically popular but do not address structural volatility.

The PSTHA exclusion of up to ten percent of general fund tax revenue, roughly twenty-five billion dollars, could be used to time spending and avoid the two-year consecutive excess that triggers rebates. This is a real governance concern. The funds still must be appropriated eventually and count toward the Gann limit when withdrawn. It is not a permanent escape hatch for unlimited spending.

The Budget Center notes that without this change, the 20% cap would be unusable during boom years when revenues near the Gann limit. The constitutional requirement forces deposits until that level is reached.

Opponents claim the proposition guarantees more spending. The LAO analysis contradicts this. It shows reserves would actually be higher.

The expanded debt payments cover existing obligations rather than new programs. Paying down the roughly twenty billion dollars in federal UI debt would reduce employer tax burdens and provide a clear economic benefit.

A claim that politicians would suspend deposits immediately after passage needs verification. Budget emergencies can already suspend deposits under current law.

The claim that politicians would suspend deposits immediately is not a valid argument against the proposition. It would instead demonstrate weak political will, which constitutional rules are meant to address. Suspending deposits during a declared emergency is the intended safety valve.

Opponents correctly note that the proposition does not create new funding for education, healthcare, or public safety. It only establishes capacity to maintain existing funding during downturns. Supporters who claim it protects schools are overstating its effect, but the underlying mechanism remains valuable.

Prop 98 education funding is explicitly preserved in the capital gains formula. Education's share is excluded from the revenue split.

The claim that larger reserves increase budget volatility is unsupported by fiscal analysis. The LAO, SPUR, and Budget Center all agree that higher reserves reduce spending volatility.

Raising the cap would delay mandatory infrastructure spending. California has large infrastructure needs.

Infrastructure can be funded through bonds and dedicated revenues, but operating reserves cannot be easily substituted. The state has struggled more with operating deficits than with a constitutional inability to fund infrastructure. Once the 20% cap is reached, the infrastructure requirement returns.

The expansion of debt payments to include UI loans, Medi-Cal loans, and Prop 98 settle-ups still pays real obligations.

Paying down UI debt is widely viewed as urgent because it carries interest and higher employer taxes. Extending the debt payment requirement to 2040 is a net positive for debt reduction compared to making it optional in 2030.

The binary choice favors larger reserves. Tighter withdrawal rules are not on the ballot, so raising the ceiling is preferable to keeping smaller reserves under the same constraints.

Locking money in reserves does mean deferring current spending on housing, education, and healthcare. However, the proposition only raises the ceiling and increases deposits during windfalls. The existing 1.5% annual set-aside remains unchanged.

The marginal new saving comes from excess capital gains in boom years, exactly when the state should avoid committing to ongoing spending. The main beneficiaries of a "no" vote are taxpayers who might receive rare Gann-limit rebates, those who prefer immediate infrastructure spending, and anyone who wants the Gann limit to act as a binding constraint on government size. The main beneficiaries of a "yes" vote are lower-income recipients of state services during recessions.

The LAO has explicitly stated that the ten percent cap is insufficient for California's revenue volatility. The main objection treats one-time rebates as more valuable than recession buffers. Nonpartisan fiscal analysis strongly supports a yes vote.

California's documented boom-bust cycle and fifth-place volatility ranking underscore the need for larger reserves. The ten percent cap covers roughly thirty percent of a typical downturn gap, while twenty percent would cover about half. Counting deposits as spending under the Gann limit is economically backwards and prevents saving exactly when it is most needed. The proposition has broad support from fiscal analysts, firefighters, hospitals, chambers of commerce, PTA groups, and editorial boards across major newspapers.

Opposition is largely partisan and overstates the measure as a spending increase. The final recommendation is yes. Several caveats do not change this conclusion: supporters overstate protections for education, healthcare, and public safety; withdrawal rules remain somewhat loose; the PSTHA Gann exclusion is a bounded workaround; twenty percent reserves may still be insufficient for severe multi-year downturns; and political discipline to actually deposit funds rather than declare emergencies remains a risk.

I am weighing normative judgment against the evidence. The nonpartisan LAO analysis shows Prop 2 raises the BSA cap to 20% of general fund tax revenues, requires larger deposits when capital gains exceed the prior threshold, extends extra debt payments through 2040, and expands eligible debt to include federal UI loans, Prop 98 settle-ups, and Medi-Cal loans.

Deposits into the BSA and PSTHA do not count toward the Gann limit, but withdrawals do. The May Revision process could also serve as a budget emergency proclamation.

The LAO projects higher reserves and more debt payments under Prop 2. This would ease balancing when revenues decline.

An independent expert consensus supports the change. The LAO report finds the current 10% reserve covers only about 30% of future budget gaps. A 20% reserve would cover roughly half. California ranks fifth in revenue volatility yet twenty-eighth in reserve levels. The current structure is insufficient.

SPUR endorses the proposition.

The Budget & Policy Center, Sacramento Bee, McClatchy, PTA, California Professional Firefighters, hospitals, and the Los Angeles Chamber of Commerce also support the proposition. The SF Chronicle endorses it but warns that politicians must actually use the reserves. One Republican, Josh Hoover, voted yes and co-wrote a support op-ed. Most opposition comes from Republican legislators and groups such as Reform California and the California Policy Center.

David Crane criticizes the withdrawal rules as too loose. He warns that a larger reserve could let governors bake in spending and reduce taxpayer rebates.

The main objection about a slush fund is being evaluated. The withdrawal rules are unchanged from Prop 2 of 2014. A governor must declare a budget emergency. The legislature must approve any withdrawal. Normally only half the balance can be taken out.

The budget emergency declaration is a pre-existing feature, not created by this proposition. A larger reserve does not make withdrawals easier; it simply increases the pool of funds available under the same rules. The alternative of not saving would spend money immediately during boom years, which actually worsens volatility.

The most substantive objection is the Gann limit loophole and its effect on taxpayer rebates.

The Gann limit loophole is being examined more closely. Under current law, reserve deposits count as appropriations subject to the limit, while withdrawals do not. Prop 2 reverses this for BSA and PSTHA. This means surplus years near the limit could be saved rather than refunded to taxpayers or spent on infrastructure. Whether this is harmful is still being weighed.

Taxpayer rebates under the Gann limit are rare. The limit has been modified many times and rarely binds. When it does bind, one-time rebates would sacrifice reserves that protect schools and services during downturns. Schools already have Prop 98 protection and a dedicated reserve. One-time rebates are politically popular but do not address structural volatility.

The PSTHA exclusion of up to ten percent of general fund tax revenue, roughly twenty-five billion dollars, could be used to time spending and avoid the two-year consecutive excess that triggers rebates. This is a real governance concern. The funds still must be appropriated eventually and count toward the Gann limit when withdrawn. It is not a permanent escape hatch for unlimited spending.

The Budget Center notes that without this change, the 20% cap would be unusable during boom years when revenues near the Gann limit. The constitutional requirement forces deposits until that level is reached.

Opponents claim the proposition guarantees more spending. The LAO analysis contradicts this. It shows reserves would actually be higher.

The expanded debt payments cover existing obligations rather than new programs. Paying down the roughly twenty billion dollars in federal UI debt would reduce employer tax burdens and provide a clear economic benefit.

A claim that politicians would suspend deposits immediately after passage needs verification. Budget emergencies can already suspend deposits under current law.

The claim that politicians would suspend deposits immediately is not a valid argument against the proposition. It would instead demonstrate weak political will, which constitutional rules are meant to address. Suspending deposits during a declared emergency is the intended safety valve.

Opponents correctly note that the proposition does not create new funding for education, healthcare, or public safety. It only establishes capacity to maintain existing funding during downturns. Supporters who claim it protects schools are overstating its effect, but the underlying mechanism remains valuable.

Prop 98 education funding is explicitly preserved in the capital gains formula. Education's share is excluded from the revenue split.

The claim that larger reserves increase budget volatility is unsupported by fiscal analysis. The LAO, SPUR, and Budget Center all agree that higher reserves reduce spending volatility.

Raising the cap would delay mandatory infrastructure spending. California has large infrastructure needs.

Infrastructure can be funded through bonds and dedicated revenues, but operating reserves cannot be easily substituted. The state has struggled more with operating deficits than with a constitutional inability to fund infrastructure. Once the 20% cap is reached, the infrastructure requirement returns.

The expansion of debt payments to include UI loans, Medi-Cal loans, and Prop 98 settle-ups still pays real obligations.

Paying down UI debt is widely viewed as urgent because it carries interest and higher employer taxes. Extending the debt payment requirement to 2040 is a net positive for debt reduction compared to making it optional in 2030.

The binary choice favors larger reserves. Tighter withdrawal rules are not on the ballot, so raising the ceiling is preferable to keeping smaller reserves under the same constraints.

Locking money in reserves does mean deferring current spending on housing, education, and healthcare. However, the proposition only raises the ceiling and increases deposits during windfalls. The existing 1.5% annual set-aside remains unchanged.

The marginal new saving comes from excess capital gains in boom years, exactly when the state should avoid committing to ongoing spending. The main beneficiaries of a "no" vote are taxpayers who might receive rare Gann-limit rebates, those who prefer immediate infrastructure spending, and anyone who wants the Gann limit to act as a binding constraint on government size. The main beneficiaries of a "yes" vote are lower-income recipients of state services during recessions.

The LAO has explicitly stated that the ten percent cap is insufficient for California's revenue volatility. The main objection treats one-time rebates as more valuable than recession buffers. Nonpartisan fiscal analysis strongly supports a yes vote.

California's documented boom-bust cycle and fifth-place volatility ranking underscore the need for larger reserves. The ten percent cap covers roughly thirty percent of a typical downturn gap, while twenty percent would cover about half. Counting deposits as spending under the Gann limit is economically backwards and prevents saving exactly when it is most needed. The proposition has broad support from fiscal analysts, firefighters, hospitals, chambers of commerce, PTA groups, and editorial boards across major newspapers.

Opposition is largely partisan and overstates the measure as a spending increase. The final recommendation is yes. Several caveats do not change this conclusion: supporters overstate protections for education, healthcare, and public safety; withdrawal rules remain somewhat loose; the PSTHA Gann exclusion is a bounded workaround; twenty percent reserves may still be insufficient for severe multi-year downturns; and political discipline to actually deposit funds rather than declare emergencies remains a risk.","format":"xai-responses-v1","index":0},{"type":"reasoning.encrypted","data":".eyJlbmRwb2ludF9zbHVnIjoieC1haS9ncm9rLTQuNy0yMDI2MDkxNnx4YWkifQ","format":"xai-responses-v1","id":"rs_7c349573-0bc1-9244-aaa0-fc194a652232","index":1}]
